comparedAgainst: Wikipedia, Relational database (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relational_database): defines relations/tuples/keys (candidate, primary, foreign, surrogate, composite) and 1:N/M:N cardinality with one diagram and no SQL; reference material, not a tutorial -- no runnable code, no worked schema, no exercises, no engine-specific behavior.

GeeksforGeeks, Types of Keys in Relational Model (https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dbms/types-of-keys-in-relational-model-candidate-super-primary-alternate-and-foreign/): ten key types over STUDENT/STUDENT_COURSE toy tables with several diagrams, but no SQL syntax, no runnable code, no exercises, no discussion of enforcement, NULL behavior, or cross-engine differences.

IBM, What is a relational database? (https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/relational-databases): covers tables, primary/foreign keys and ACID at an overview level with one SQL join example; no candidate-key discussion, no diagrams, no exercises, no constraint-violation demonstrations.

Sources spot-checked, not competitors: E. F. Codd's 1970 paper (the 'relation... in its accepted mathematical sense' and 'nonredundant... superfluous' passages, both fetched and confirmed verbatim), sqlite.org pragma.html (foreign_keys is a no-op inside a transaction) and partialindex.html ('uniqueness across some subset of the rows'), and learn.microsoft.com's primary-and-foreign-key-constraints page ('frequently defined on an identity column') -- all quotes in the article match the live pages.
justification: As a low-value-content reviewer this page is the opposite of thin, padded, templated or copied, and it clearly outperforms the pages that actually rank for 'relational database explained' (Wikipedia's reference-only treatment, GeeksforGeeks' diagram-heavy but code-free walkthrough, IBM's shallow overview). The seven-rule library brief is a real, specific design problem worked start to finish with a schema (member, book, copy, author, book_author, loan) that no competitor builds, every CREATE TABLE and constraint violation is executable SQL with verified output (run-code.mjs passes, 70 blocks/41 executed), and the four exercises vary in form (derive-the-key, predict-four-verdicts, write-a-CHECK-and-test-it-against-edge-cases, design-a-new-table) rather than repeating one template. Sourcing is genuinely primary and accurate: Codd's 1970 paper is quoted directly and correctly ('in its accepted mathematical sense', the nonredundant-key definition, the self-referencing-relation remark), the Silberschatz slides are cited for the NULL warning, and eleven SQLite/PostgreSQL/SQL Server documentation pages are cited at the exact claims they support (spot-checked: the foreign_keys pragma being a transaction no-op, the partial-index wording, the 'frequently defined on an identity column' quote) -- every source in front matter is cited inline at least once, satisfying the pilot-round lesson. Distinctive sentences and the Codd quotations came back clean on web search: no copied or closely paraphrased passages from any tutorial site. Structurally the page reads nothing like its siblings: headings ('A relation is a set of rows; a table only resembles one', 'What declarations cannot say') are specific to this content, not the boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion pattern, and the opening delivers the seven rules immediately with no filler; the toolchain sentence is deliberately the third paragraph, not a stamped opener. The library schema is intentionally reused across the pillar (CONTENT_PLAN's own stated angle for this article, 'one schema reused across the pillar'), and rather than duplicating sql-joins.md, the two are complementary and cross-aware: sql-joins.md uses a deliberately cut-down two-table version (nullable member_id, denormalized title) and this article's 'The slip with no name on it' section explicitly names and contrasts that design choice, which is thoughtful reuse, not lazy duplication. docs/crosslinks/databases/relational-model-and-keys.md exists with three specific, sensible pending links (indexes, normalization, transactions-and-acid), so the missing-sibling-link problem that cost the pilot round's articles points does not apply here. The only gap found: the 1NF atomic-attribute claim is stated as 'the textbook model asks for' without an inline citation at that sentence, even though the concept is well-known and uncontroversial. That single minor nit, plus the diagram-heavy, code-light competing pages this beats decisively, keeps the score just below a 'clearly better than any result, no notes' 9.5+ rather than at MDN-with-nits.

issues.location: "Many-to-many needs a third table" section, the sentence "the textbook model asks for attribute values to be **atomic**, indivisible, for this reason"
issues.problem: This is presented as a rule of the relational model but has no inline citation at the point the claim is made, unlike almost every other non-obvious claim on the page. The term is also the crosslink target for the future normalization article, so a reader who wants to verify or read further has nowhere to go yet.
